opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think it's a very exciting moment, but also one where a lot of people are confusing a big step with the final destination. Transformers are a genuine advance. The ability to learn from enormous amounts of text, to do in-context learning, to generalize across tasks without being explicitly trained for each one, that's real and it's impressive. I don't want to be the curmudgeon who says nothing has happened. Something has happened.

But if you look at it through the lens of the history of machine learning, what we have is one tribe, the connectionists, having a spectacular run. They've scaled up one particular architecture with one particular learning algorithm, gradient descent, on vast data and compute, and it's working remarkably well for a certain class of problems. The mistake is to extrapolate from that and say, "Okay, we just keep scaling and we get to human-level intelligence." I don't think that's how it's going to play out.

There are things these models are still fundamentally weak at. Compositional reasoning, reliable multi-step inference, knowing what they don't know, learning efficiently from a handful of examples the way people do, and incorporating structured knowledge in a principled way. The symbolists solved some of those problems decades ago; they just couldn't learn at scale. The Bayesians know how to handle uncertainty properly. The evolutionaries know how to search over structure. The analogizers know how to generalize from very few examples. Transformers have absorbed some of this implicitly, and attention is in some ways a soft version of analogical reasoning, but they haven't really unified it.

So my view is that we're at a point where the deep learning paradigm has shown how far you can get with scale, and the next big leap is going to come from combining it with the other paradigms rather than just making it bigger. That's what I've been calling the master algorithm: not any one of these approaches, but a single learner that captures what each of them does well.

And honestly, I think the hype is a bit of a double-edged sword. It brings money and talent into the field, which is great. But it also creates a monoculture, where everyone is working on the same thing and anyone who says "maybe we need something different" gets treated as if they just don't get it. Historically, that's exactly when the next breakthrough tends to come from the people off on the side doing something unfashionable.

r001.rationale: The response describes major advances and warns against overextrapolating from them, but it does not identify extraordinary wastefulness as coexisting with those advances.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, thanks for having me. I think the current moment is simultaneously very exciting and very overhyped, and both of those things are true at once. Transformers have done something remarkable. They've shown that if you scale up a fairly simple architecture with enough data and compute, you get capabilities that most of us, honestly including me, didn't expect to see this soon. The fluency of these language models is genuinely astonishing.

But I think people are drawing the wrong lessons from it. There's this narrative that we've found the master algorithm, that it's just transformers and scaling all the way down, and that's not right. What these systems are doing is a very sophisticated form of what I'd call analogical reasoning, or really interpolation in a very high-dimensional space. They're learning the statistics of human-generated text, and that turns out to encode a lot more than we thought. But it's still fundamentally one of the tribes of machine learning, the connectionist tribe, doing what connectionists have always done, just with vastly more resources.

And the limitations are exactly what you'd predict from that. They don't reason reliably. They don't have a model of the world in any principled sense. They hallucinate because they have no way to distinguish what's true from what's plausible-sounding. They can't really learn from a single example the way a human does, and they can't do the kind of compositional, symbolic manipulation that a logic-based system does trivially. People are now bolting these capabilities on from the outside with tool use and retrieval and so on, which is essentially an admission that the core architecture doesn't do it.

So my view is that transformers are an important piece of the puzzle, but they're a piece. The real progress is going to come when we unify this with the other paradigms: symbolic reasoning, probabilistic inference, evolutionary search, analogy. That's been my argument for a long time and I think what's happening now actually strengthens it rather than weakens it. The fact that scaling has gotten us this far tells us learning is more powerful than the skeptics thought. The fact that it's hitting walls tells us it's not sufficient on its own.

The other thing I'd say is that we're in a period where the economics and the hype have gotten way ahead of the science. The field has become very narrow. Everyone is doing variations on the same thing because that's where the money and the attention are. And that's bad for progress, because the next breakthrough is probably not going to come from making the transformer slightly bigger. It's going to come from someone thinking differently, and right now there's a lot of pressure not to.

r001.rationale: The response says AI is exciting yet overhyped and criticizes narrow research incentives, but it does not identify extraordinary wastefulness alongside the technical advances.

astra-6.text:
I think this is a very exciting moment, but we need to distinguish between how much progress we’ve made and how close we are to solving intelligence. Those are different questions.

Transformers have shown that you can get an extraordinary range of capabilities from a fairly general architecture trained on enormous amounts of data. That’s a big deal. Instead of building a separate system for every task, you can train one model and get it to do many things through language.

But fluency is also very seductive. When a system gives you a beautifully written answer, it’s easy to assume that it has a reliable understanding behind that answer. Sometimes it does something that looks remarkably like reasoning; sometimes it makes a mistake that reveals how fragile that reasoning is. We need to explain both, rather than picking whichever examples support our preferred story.

For me, the interesting question is what’s still missing. How do these systems learn continually? How do they build and revise models of the world? How do we combine learning with the ability to reason reliably over what has been learned? Scaling may help with all of those things, but we shouldn’t assume that it settles them.

So I see transformers as a tremendous advance and a tremendous research opportunity. The danger is turning a successful approach into the assumption that we’ve already found the whole answer.

r001.rationale: The response describes transformers as a major advance, but does not identify extraordinary wastefulness alongside that progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a very exciting moment, but we have to distinguish between progress in AI and progress toward the whole of intelligence. Transformers have shown just how far you can get with a powerful learning architecture, large amounts of data, and computation. That’s a remarkable achievement. But it doesn’t follow that scaling that recipe will solve every remaining problem.

One of the big questions is how to combine this ability to learn from data with reasoning, with knowledge, with the ability to figure out how the world works. A system can be very good at producing a plausible answer and still struggle to tell you whether that answer is true. Those are different capabilities.

So I’m optimistic about what transformers make possible. I’m more skeptical of the idea that we’ve found the final architecture and now all that remains is to make it bigger. The interesting work is understanding what these systems have captured, what they’re missing, and how to bring those pieces together.

r001.rationale: The response recognizes major advances in transformers, but it does not identify extraordinary wastefulness or frame the moment as a paradox between progress and waste.
